issues.legal_issue: A land acquisition officer must make an award for land covered by a valid acquisition notification and declaration unless the land is formally withdrawn from acquisition.
material_facts: Two parcels were covered by an acquisition notification and declaration for a public bus station.
The land acquisition officer made an award for one parcel but omitted the other after being informed of a private settlement concerning it.
The omitted parcel had not been formally withdrawn from acquisition.
issues.conclusion: The land acquisition officer had no authority to omit the parcel from the award on the basis of the private settlement; an award was required for all land notified and declared unless it was withdrawn in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 4, 6, 11 and 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, once the notification and declaration have been made, the land acquisition officer must make an award for the notified land unless it is withdrawn under Section 48. A private settlement does not itself authorize the officer to omit land from the award. No earlier case is relied on for this proposition.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the acquisition of land for a stated public purpose.
predicates.land_covered_by_notification_and_declara: The land was included in the acquisition notification and the subsequent declaration.
predicates.land_formally_withdrawn: The land was formally withdrawn from acquisition through the legally prescribed process.

issues.definition: When a land acquisition proceeding concerns land included in a notification and declaration, and that land has not been formally withdrawn, an award is required for it.

issues.legal_issue: An omission from the award concerning one parcel does not, by itself, require quashing the acquisition of a separate parcel where the public purpose for that separate parcel remains genuine.
material_facts: The award covered the parcel claimed by the appellant but omitted a different notified parcel because of a private settlement involving that other parcel.
The appellant did not dispute the stated public purpose for acquiring the parcel claimed by him.
The settlement provided land for the same stated purpose, and there was no material showing that the remaining acquisition was unnecessary or that its stated purpose was unreal.
The appellant challenged the acquisition only after the award had been made.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition of the appellant’s parcel was not liable to be quashed merely because the award omitted the other parcel.
issues.legal_principle: Although the land acquisition officer was required to make an award for all notified land unless it was withdrawn under Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, that error did not establish that the acquisition of the appellant’s separate parcel was unnecessary or contrary to law or public interest. The Court relied on the continuing public purpose and the absence of material disproving the genuine need; it cited no earlier case for this conclusion.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A person challenges the acquisition of land for a public purpose.
predicates.award_omitted_a_different_notified_parce: The award omitted a notified parcel other than the parcel whose acquisition is challenged.
predicates.challenged_parcel_has_genuine_public_pur: The acquisition of the challenged parcel continues to serve the stated public purpose.
predicates.no_material_shows_challenged_parcel_unne: The record contains no material showing that the challenged parcel is unnecessary for the stated purpose.

issues.definition: If a land acquisition challenge concerns a parcel with a genuine public purpose, omission of a different notified parcel from the award does not require the challenged parcel’s acquisition to be quashed when there is no material showing it is unnecessary.

issues.legal_issue: A claim that a land acquisition was motivated by bad faith cannot succeed without adequate material supporting the alleged improper motive.
material_facts: The appellant alleged that the acquisition was intended to benefit a housing society and persons interested in a neighboring parcel.

There was no material showing that the acquisition notification was issued at the instance of those persons, that the acquiring authority acted at their instance, or that the need for the public facility was not genuine.
issues.conclusion: The allegation of bad faith was not established, and the acquisition was not invalidated on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: A finding of bad faith requires adequate supporting material. The Court found no evidence connecting the acquisition to the alleged beneficiaries or disproving the genuine public need. No earlier case is relied on for this conclusion.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A person challenges the acquisition of land for a public purpose.
predicates.no_material_links_acquisition_to_alleged: The record contains no material showing that the acquisition or acquiring authority acted at the instance of the alleged beneficiaries.
predicates.no_material_disproves_genuine_public_nee: The record contains no material showing that the stated public need was not genuine.

issues.definition: In a land acquisition challenge, bad faith is not established where the record neither links the acquisition to alleged beneficiaries nor disproves the genuine public need.

issues.legal_issue: The exercise of discretionary judicial power in land acquisition challenges requires consideration of public and private interests, and relief is not warranted merely because a legal point is raised.
material_facts: The case was a challenge to a land acquisition for a public bus station.
The acquisition had been challenged years after the notification, and the stated public purpose remained in place.
The High Court declined to interfere, and the Supreme Court concluded that the acquisition did not warrant interference on the facts.
issues.conclusion: Courts should weigh public interest against private interest when considering discretionary relief in land acquisition proceedings; quashing the acquisition is not the only possible way to remedy a legal wrong.
issues.legal_principle: The power under Article 226 of the Constitution is discretionary and is to be exercised in furtherance of justice, not merely because a legal point is made out. In land acquisition matters, courts must weigh public interest against private interest. Where an acquisition is found legally deficient, an appropriate remedy may be available without quashing the acquisition. No earlier case is relied on for these observations.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A person challenges an acquisition of land for a public purpose.
predicates.discretionary_relief_requested: The challenger asks the court to grant relief that is within its discretion.
predicates.public_and_private_interests_are_relevan: The requested relief affects both the public purpose of the acquisition and the private interests of affected persons.

issues.definition: When discretionary relief is sought in a land acquisition challenge affecting public and private interests, the court must balance those interests in deciding whether and what relief to grant.
